desc:
A frog sits on the first of several stones in a row; heights[i] is the height of stone i. In one jump the frog moves to the next stone or skips one stone (from index i to i + 1 or i + 2). A jump from stone i to stone j costs |heights[i] - heights[j]| energy.

Return the minimum total energy needed to reach the last stone. If there is only one stone the answer is 0.

Example: for [10, 30, 40, 20] the best route is 10 → 30 → 20 with cost 20 + 10 = 30.
hints: Think about the final jump: the frog lands on the last stone coming from one of two stones.
Let best(i) be the least energy to reach stone i. Then best(i) = min(best(i-1) + |h[i]-h[i-1]|, best(i-2) + |h[i]-h[i-2]|).
best(0) = 0 and best(1) = |h[1] - h[0]|. Only the last two values of best are ever needed, so two variables are enough.
editorial: Let best(i) be the minimum energy to stand on stone i. The frog arrives at stone i either from i-1 or from i-2, and whatever happened before that must itself be optimal, so best(i) = min(best(i-1) + |h[i] - h[i-1]|, best(i-2) + |h[i] - h[i-2]|) with best(0) = 0.

The first stone has no predecessor, so for i = 1 only the first option exists. The answer is best(n-1). One pass with two rolling variables gives O(n) time and O(1) space. A recursive version without memoisation would take exponential time because the same prefixes are evaluated over and over.
